title: The Welcome My Father-in-Law Gave Me

paragraphs: The election contest between my Children's Reform Association and my friend Thyagarasan's Youth Association was in full swing. Three days before the election, the Youth Association staged a play. At Thyagarasan's house, the man who was to play the hero quarrelled and walked away. Tickets had already been sold at a quarter anna each. Thyagarasan came running to me in distress.

I immediately laid down a condition. "I will take a role in the play. In return, you must withdraw from the election contest." He agreed. The election ended then and there. The play began. I acted as Dushyanta and won applause. With that, the Youth Association was dissolved; everything became the Children's Reform Association—and before long that too disappeared!

The reason for that disappearance was my political involvement. Organizations formed for the welfare of the South drew me powerfully. The force of the anti-Hindi movement that began in 1938 urged me to stand in the ranks of the Tamil Brigade. Though I did not get the chance to plunge into it with all my strength, I began carrying a flag among those who marched shouting, "Long live Tamil!" and "Down with Hindi!"

There was one meeting addressed by the late warrior Anjanenjan Alagirisami. I proudly say that it was that meeting which made me "Karunanidhi". The speech Alagiri delivered, sounding the war-drum for the soldiers defending Tamil, still echoes in my ears. For more than an hour a storm blew across the stage. The sound of revolution reached the sky. It was a roar as though a thousand lions had gathered and thundered at once. "Will Hindi dominate Tamil Nadu? Come, all of you—come, Tamils!" he cried and raged.

When the meeting ended, he vomited blood. He fainted and collapsed. He writhed, unable to bear the pain in his lower abdomen and ribs. I asked what was wrong. They said he was ill. I asked why, if he was ill, he had to shout like that. My question reached Alagiri's ears. He embraced me affectionately and said, even while enduring the pain, "Brother, this country is sicker than I am! If a doctor has a cold, can he neglect a gravely ill patient? That is how I work."

Those words are what have made me stand before you today as a worker in the cause. Alagiri was not close to me then; I had not met him often. Yet he stole my heart. I became captive to Alagiri's passionate fervour for his principles.

A dissatisfaction began to burn within me: was it enough that only a few hundred students should read what we wrote in a handwritten journal? I longed to see my writing climb aboard the vehicle of print. At that time Arignar Anna had begun the journal Dravida Nadu from Kanchipuram. Imagine my delight if an article of mine appeared in its third or fourth issue! I was only a school student. I had moved from writing and reading my own words for my own pleasure to a stage where tens and hundreds of people could read and praise them.

On impulse I wrote an article and sent it to "Dravida Nadu, Kanchipuram." The very next week it appeared. I praised myself inwardly, imagining people across the country reading and enjoying my piece. Rajagopal, who stood by me and had an unshakable attachment to the movement, shed tears of joy when he saw it. For a whole week I went around Tiruvarur with the paper in my hand. I cannot describe that happiness. Wherever four people were sitting and talking, I would go with the journal, chat for a while, then casually put it down. I would sit there eagerly, waiting for someone to pick it up and read my article. Only after they read it and praised me would I leave.

Even now, when I remember that day of immense joy, happiness surges through me. Do you know the title of the article that threw me into such excitement? "Youth Sacrifice!" Yes—that was its title. Without even realizing it, I had already declared through that title that I was ready to sacrifice my youth for my country. The next week I sent another article, titled "Rationalist Paramasivam." It was not published.

The following week Arignar Anna came to Tiruvarur to take part in a Nabi Nayagam festival. Until then I had never met Anna. He was staying at the house of T. N. Raman, one of the pillars of the movement. Anna asked, "Who is this Karunanidhi in this town? Bring him here. I want to see him." I was taken to him. The moment he saw me, Anna was astonished. He had not expected Karunanidhi to be such a tiny boy. "Are you studying?" he asked. "I am," I replied in a trembling voice. "From now on, don't write any more articles and send them to me!" he said rather sternly. I was stunned.

For more than twenty-seven years after that day, the Anna who advised me and embraced me with affection remained an elder brother not born with me, a rare leader, a god of love who showed me affection beyond even that of a brother born of the same mother, a mother greater than my own mother—and even today, my ideal made flesh. I rejoice when I think of it. Through that joy falls a curtain of tears. Upon that curtain, in golden letters, shine the words: "One needs a heart that can bear anything."

Yet the movement-frenzy that rose in me even against the advice of that temple of affection, Anna, put a full stop to my school life. To raise funds for the Tamil Nadu Tamil Students' Association, we staged in Tiruvarur a play I had written and acted in, Palaniyappan. The cost of staging it was two hundred rupees. The collection was eighty rupees. Heavy rain produced that result and left us stranded in midstream. We had to clear a debt that had crossed one hundred rupees. What were we to do? Wherever we went, creditors stood before us. I had never learned the new lesson that repaying a debt was uncivilized, nor did I wish to learn it.

Thennan and I sat and cried. Creditors came right into the theatre shed and surrounded us. The actress who played the heroine had to be paid her salary and given money for her journey home. There seemed no way out. During the play a friend had presented me with a silver cup worth twenty rupees. We gave that cup to the actress and sent her on her way. But how were we to settle the remaining debt? On Thennan's suggestion, without telling anyone, we ran to Nagapattinam.

There we approached R. V. Gopal, the Dravidar Kazhagam leader, and explained our plight. He was very fond of me, but lending a hundred rupees made him pause. Friends there, Pakkirisami and Malaikozhundu, recommended us. In the end we got the hundred rupees. How did it come? Mr. R. V. Gopal was about to start the Nagai Dravidian Actors' Association. He bought our play Palaniyappan for one hundred rupees for that association. That was how the money came. My first play, Palaniyappan, was later staged in many places under the title Santa; and that same play, under the name Natchuk Koppai, continues to be staged in many places even today.

Once a play had been sold, my desire grew. I thought I could write and sell many more plays, make that my livelihood, and at the same time use them as an effective instrument of propaganda for good principles. I began writing at a furious pace. My family and relatives stood in the way. "It is enough if you get some office job and earn fifty rupees a month. Try for that!" they began urging me. Taking a job felt like poison. My peace of mind vanished. On top of that, the thought that I was sitting at home as nothing but another mouth to feed began to gnaw at me.

And in the midst of this disgrace, did love also have to become a trouble? It too arrived. With love came restraint as well. I decided that I would take a young woman's hand and begin life's journey. She agreed. Then the parents intervened. Forces gathered on both sides. In the end, love lost.

The chief reason for that defeat was simply this: I was a Self-Respecter. She was married to another man by priestly rites. The echo in my heart after that failure in love was the very play that began as Palaniyappan and became Natchuk Koppai. Seeing me broken-hearted, my family set out at once to find me a bride.

Someone was waiting for me in Chidambaram—the beloved younger sister of the musician Chidambaram Jayaraman. My relative Raja Santhanam and my sisters went to see the bride. Her family gave their consent. From Chidambaram they sent a telegram asking me to come immediately. Thennan and I set out.

What monthly income did I have to marry and run a household? Should I not first sit down in some job and only then get married? My thoughts ran faster than the train. Chidambaram station arrived. Thennan and I hired a horse cart and reached the bride's house. We stepped through the doorway. A huge voice rang out: "Mahamayi! Mother!" Startled, we looked up. On the verandah sat a mountain-like figure. Yes—he was the bride's father, Sundaranar, a master of music and a noted singer. I had come to see his beloved daughter.
